title: 95% of Vietnamese Want Change—Here's How It's Actually Happening
excerpt: New enforcement data and disappearing dog meat markets show Vietnam's cultural shift is real. In just months, major cities have shuttered longtime trade hubs while public backing for change hits historic highs.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam is at an inflection point. Ho Chi Minh City's iconic dog meat streets have vanished, enforcement actions are accelerating, and public opposition has reached 95%—driven not by international pressure alone, but by Vietnamese themselves, especially younger generations who reject the trade as incompatible with modern Vietnam.

Key Findings

Ho Chi Minh City's Dog Meat Streets Are Now Ghost Alleys

By August 2026, Alley 189 on Cong Quynh—once a well-known dog meat hub—has effectively closed, with its last restaurant shuttering in early 2026. The owner, like dozens of others across the city's former red-light zones for the trade, has pivoted to goat meat and other dishes. This isn't isolated: across Hanoi, by July 2026, 28 facilities had stopped operating entirely and 25 more had registered to change their business model. The market isn't just shrinking—it's structurally collapsing in urban centers.

What's driving this isn't regulation alone; it's generational attitude change. Survey data cited in recent reporting shows 91% of Vietnamese now oppose the dog and cat meat trade, and 95% said consuming dog or cat meat is not part of Vietnamese culture. This reframing—from "tradition" to "not-tradition"—represents a seismic cultural shift happening in real time.

Enforcement Is Tightening: The Hung Yen Case Shows Why

On August 8, 2026, police in Hung Yen Province discovered 150 kg of slaughtered dog meat in a residential freezer, with no invoices, origin documents, or traceability records. The owner admitted to buying and collecting it for resale. This case exemplifies a critical vulnerability: the dog meat supply chain remains completely unregulated, making it a public health liability that governments can no longer ignore. As of August 1, 2026, new veterinary enforcement rules (Decree 204/2026/ND-CP) tripled penalties for violations involving disease-carrying animals and untraced products, signaling that authorities are using food safety and disease prevention as enforcement levers.

Rabies Crisis Crystallizes the Health Case Against the Trade

In the first six months of 2026, Thái Nguyên Province alone reported 8,077 people needing rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, including 560 requiring antiserum. Nationwide, 39 people died of rabies in 2026 across 18 provinces, a crisis driven by uncontrolled dog populations and the absence of traceability in the meat supply. Without knowing the origin of dog meat—whether from vaccinated animals, strays, or stolen pets—the trade becomes a vector for disease. This health reality, combined with the 95% public opposition noted above, creates political space for enforcement that governments are now occupying.

New Penalty Framework Closes the Enforcement Gap

Decree 204/2026/ND-CP and Decree 211/2026/NĐ-CP, both effective August 1–5, 2026, raised maximum fines to VND 100 million for individuals and VND 200 million for organizations in violation of livestock and veterinary regulations. More importantly, these decrees specifically target untraced, disease-bearing animal products—which describes the dog meat supply chain perfectly. The shift from moral argument to regulatory enforcement removes the trade's legal ambiguity.

Pet Theft Rings Are Under Pressure from Public Vigilance

Pet theft remains a major pipeline into the trade, but public awareness is rising. Residents in Bình Định, Cần Thơ, and other provinces reported coordinated dog-stealing operations since June 2026, leading to police interventions. More significantly, in August 2026, community members in An Giang Province actively pursued suspected pet thieves, forcing police to intervene. This vigilantism reflects growing public intolerance—Vietnamese are mobilizing to protect their own animals, signaling that the social license for the trade is collapsing from within.

Also Worth Noting

  • New Public Safety Rules Enforce Rabies Control — August 2026 regulations impose fines of VND 1–2 million for dogs in public without muzzles, leashes, or supervision, tightening the regulatory architecture around dog ownership and management.
  • Stray Dog Control Campaigns Expand Across Provinces — Lam Dong and Bac Ha launched coordinated stray dog management in early August 2026, part of a broader shift toward humane population control rather than slaughter-based models.
  • Draft Food Safety Law Under National Assembly Review — Vietnam's replacement Food Safety Law, notified to the WTO on August 3, 2026, includes strengthened traceability and supply-chain controls, creating additional pressure on unregulated meat sources including dog.
  • Youth Leadership on Cultural Identity — Recent reporting emphasizes that younger Vietnamese are driving the shift against the trade, redefining what "Vietnamese culture" actually means in 2026—a bottom-up reclamation that authorities are now validating through policy.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030. When 95% of Vietnamese want change, the question is no longer if, but how fast we can make it happen.

Vietnamese are rewriting their own story about what culture means in 2026.

In August alone, Ho Chi Minh City's famous dog meat streets disappeared. Business owners are pivoting. Enforcement penalties just tripled. And when surveyed, 95% of Vietnamese—not international activists, but Vietnamese themselves—say the dog meat trade has no place in modern Vietnam.

This is a public health crisis too: 39 people died of rabies in just six months of 2026, largely because the dog meat supply chain remains completely unregulated and untraceable. No invoices. No health records. No accountability.

But the momentum is undeniable. Younger generations reject the trade. Neighborhoods organize to stop pet theft rings. Authorities are using food safety laws as enforcement tools. The social license for the trade is collapsing from within.

**This is what real change looks like.** It's led by Vietnamese, driven by Vietnamese values, and backed by Vietnamese public support.
